column3: A huge plateau lake beside Kunming, ringed by hills. In winter, black-headed gulls arrive from Siberia and people feed them from the shore.
Gray limestone pillars rise like a petrified forest across the land, shaped over millions of years. The Sani people, a branch of the Yi, tell the legend of Ashima here.
Kunming's city-center park, with lotus ponds, willow-lined paths and old men playing chess. It is a good place to see the slow side of the Spring City.
A theme park with homes, dances and food from many of Yunnan's 25 minority peoples, a quick way to see how varied the province is.
A path carved into a cliff by hand over decades, climbing high above Dian Lake to a view over the water.
Kunming's biggest Buddhist temple, set in a sunken courtyard with a pond and a pavilion, and cherry blossoms in spring.
Two archways facing each other in the old city, a symbol of Kunming. Twice a year, at sunset, their shadows are said to meet.

A bowl of boiling-hot broth with a layer of oil that keeps it hot. You add raw meat, quail eggs, vegetables and rice noodles, and it cooks at your table. The name comes from a legend about a wife who carried lunch over a bridge to her husband.
Chicken steamed in a special clay pot with a chimney in the middle, so the soup is clean and light, with no water added.
A flaky pastry filled with edible rose petals and sugar. It is a typical Kunming gift, and is best eaten fresh.
A thin sheet of dried cow's milk cheese, grilled over charcoal and rolled with rose jam or sugar. A snack of the Bai people.
In the rainy season, markets fill with wild mushrooms, and cooks put a dozen kinds in one pot. Yunnan is a mushroom-lover's paradise, though it is best to go where cooks know what is safe.
A mooncake with a salty-sweet filling of Xuanwei ham, a Yunnan twist on the festival treat.
A walled town with cobbled streets, cafés, shops and the Cangshan range behind it. Its gates and towers are built in the Bai style.

Three stone pagodas stand side by side before the Cang Mountains, more than 1,000 years old. The tallest has 16 levels. They are the most famous view in Dali, especially with their reflection in the pool.
A big, bright lake shaped like an ear, which the Bai people call their mother lake. Cycling along its shore, with the Cangshan mountains beyond, is the best way to see it.
A range of nineteen peaks behind Dali, snowy in winter. A cable car and walking paths lead along the mountain.
A Bai town with white-walled courtyards, carved gateways and painted designs. It is known for its flatbread and its rice fields.
A fishing village on the lakeshore, now filled with guesthouses and cafés that look over the water.
A firm white Bai cheese, sliced and fried or grilled until golden, with a mild, milky taste.
Fish from Erhai, simmered in a sour and spicy broth with tomatoes and herbs, a Dali favorite.
A round flatbread with a crisp crust, baked in a clay oven, and filled with salty meat or sweet sugar.
A tea ceremony of three courses for guests: first bitter, then sweet, then with a spicy aftertaste. It stands for the stages of life.
Cloth that is tied, then dipped in a plant dye to get blue-and-white patterns, made in Zhoucheng village.
An ancient fair held every spring in Dali, where traders, herders and performers gather for horse races, songs and selling goods.
A maze of cobbled lanes, canals and wooden houses of the Naxi people, with water flowing through every street. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its lanterns glow in the evening.
A rugged mountain range with a snow-covered peak north of Lijiang, rising to about 5,600 meters. A cable car goes up to the glacier, and the lakes below are known as Blue Moon Valley.
A quieter old town than Lijiang, with a clear stream, willows and a market square where the tea-horse caravans once stopped.
A pond with a pavilion and a bridge, with the snow-capped mountain reflected in the water on a clear day.
One of the deepest gorges in the world, where the Yangtze roars between two snow mountains. Hikers can walk along the cliff trail.
A valley of milky-blue pools at the foot of the snow mountain, whose color comes from minerals in the water.
A hot pot of smoked pork ribs, a warming dish in the cold mountains.
A big, flat bread filled with ham, sugar or beans, fried until crisp on the edges.
A cool, soft jelly made of chickpea flour, served with hot chili, vinegar and herbs on a warm day.
An old music played on ancient instruments, said to preserve the sound of Tang and Song courts. The elderly musicians still perform it.
A pictographic script of the Naxi, written by priests for centuries. It is among the few picture scripts still in use in the world.
A forest valley where wild Asian elephants live. You can walk along a skybridge and watch from above, but sightings are a matter of luck.
A garden of tropical rainforest plants with palms, orchids and giant trees, set along a bend of a river.
Sticky purple rice steamed in a pineapple shell, sweet and fragrant. A Dai dish.
Fish stuffed with lemongrass and herbs, wrapped in leaves, and grilled over charcoal. A Dai specialty.
A tea that is pressed into cakes and aged, so that it gets a deep, earthy taste. Some old cakes sell for a lot of money.
The Dai New Year in April, when everyone splashes water on each other for good luck. It is a joyful, soaking festival.
A Dai dance in which the performer imitates a peacock with graceful arms and hands, in a costume with a long tail.
The largest Tibetan Buddhist monastery in Yunnan, with golden roofs on a hillside, sometimes called the little Potala. Its prayer halls are lined with bright murals.
A highland park with lakes, meadows and pine forests at about 3,500 meters, where yaks graze by the water.
A hill town with a giant golden prayer wheel at the top, and wooden houses and shops along the streets below.
Tea churned with yak butter and salt, a warm drink at altitude, which Tibetan families serve to guests.
The meat of the yak, dried, boiled or stewed. It is a lean, strong-tasting meat of the highlands.
Thousands of rice terraces carved into the mountainsides by the Hani people over 1,300 years. In winter, the flooded fields reflect the sky in colors of pink, gold and blue at dawn.
Small blocks of tofu grilled on a charcoal brazier until they puff up, then dipped in a spicy sauce, and eaten on the street.
Mengzi's take on crossing-the-bridge noodles, said to be the original, with a rich, fragrant broth.
A town in the far west near the border with Myanmar, known for volcanoes, hot springs and a long history of trade.
A village built by merchants who traded abroad, with grand houses, a library and ponds with lotus.
Fried rice cake with ham and vegetables. Legend says it saved an emperor on the run, giving it the name Great Rescue.
Yunnan grows most of China's coffee, and Baoshan's beans have a smooth, mild taste.
A strong, sweet black tea from old trees, which the Chinese call red tea.
Crisp apples grown on the high plateau of northeast Yunnan, with a sweet flavor and bright red color.
A karst landscape of lakes, lotus fields and little islands, which you can cross in a wooden boat. The Yi people live in the villages around it.
Chicken stewed with notoginseng, a medicinal root grown in Wenshan, a hearty and warming soup.
Big chunks of boiled pork, served with salt and chili, a hearty meal for Yi festivals.
A Yi festival in summer when villages light torches and bonfires, dance and wrestle through the night to chase away evil.
